setupSteps: Warm up first. 2 to 3 minutes of gentle movement (cat-cow, pelvic tilts, a few seated knee lifts). Do not go in cold.
Floor. Flat mat or carpet; avoid slippery tiles (the hips can slide).
Seat. Sit near the middle of the mat on the sitting bones. A thin folded blanket under the hips helps if the tailbone feels bony.
Starting position. Knees bent, feet flat on the floor about hip-width apart, hands beside the hips.
Support (optional). Keep a wall behind you at a lean-back distance, or loop a strap round the soles of the feet (Yoga U; snippet), or plan to hold the backs of the thighs.
Stomach. Practise on a light or empty stomach; sources note the pose presses on the stomach area.
Clothing. Stretchy pants and a fitted top so the camera sees shoulders, hips, knees and ankles; no loose kurta hiding the hips.
Camera. Phone at about hip height on a stool or shelf (about 40 to 60 cm, est.), about 2 m to the side, so the whole body from head to feet is in frame (see sections 11 and 12).

steps.title: Sit tall with knees bent
steps.action: sit with the knees bent, feet flat on the floor, hands beside the hips.
steps.feel: weight on the sitting bones, spine long.

steps.title: Hold the backs of the thighs
steps.action: place the hands behind the thighs, just above the knees, elbows slightly bent.
steps.feel: chest opening, shoulders away from the ears.
steps.breathing: breathe in as the chest lifts.

steps.title: Lean back a little
steps.action: tip the torso back a few centimetres while keeping the chest lifted; the tailbone stays heavy.
steps.feel: the front of the belly switching on; weight rolling just behind the sitting bones.

steps.title: Lift one foot
steps.action: lift one foot a few centimetres, then lower; this is the balance check (optional if steady).
steps.feel: the lifting hip flexor working, the belly firm.

steps.title: Lift both feet to shin-parallel
steps.action: lift both feet until the shins are about parallel to the floor, knees still bent.
steps.feel: belly and front-of-hip working, balance on the sitting bones.

steps.title: Reach the arms forward
steps.action: if steady, let go of the thighs and reach the arms forward, palms facing in, parallel to the floor and alongside the knees.
steps.feel: shoulders relaxed, chest lifted; the belly working harder.
steps.breathing: breathe in as the arms rise.

steps.title: Lengthen the spine
steps.action: lift the chest and the crown of the head; let the lower back stay long rather than rounding or arching hard.
steps.feel: the ribs lifting away from the hips; the tailbone heavy.

steps.title: Hold
steps.action: stay with slow nose breaths. Beginners hold 4 breaths (about 20 seconds, est.); sources range from 3 to 5 breaths, 15 to 30 seconds, and 2 to 5 breaths working up to 10.
steps.feel: a steady, strong belly and front of hip, no back or neck strain.
steps.breathing: slow nose breaths; never hold the breath.

steps.title: Lower with control
steps.action: bring the feet back to the floor on an out-breath, then the hands to the floor beside the hips.
steps.feel: legs and belly releasing, no dizziness.

steps.title: Rest and repeat
steps.action: hug the knees or sit tall and shake out the legs, then do the next round.

commonMistakes.title: Rounding the back and collapsing the chest
commonMistakes.text: Rounding the back and collapsing the chest. It puts the weight on the tailbone and the sacrum and the core switches off (Yoga International; Yoga Journal; snippets). Fix: bend the knees more, hold the thighs, lift the chest, or put the feet down.

commonMistakes.title: Straightening the legs too soon
commonMistakes.text: Straightening the legs too soon. The leg weight pulls the back into a curve. Fix: keep the knees bent until the back stays long (Liforme; Yoga International; snippets).

commonMistakes.title: Leaning back too far
commonMistakes.text: Leaning back too far. The belly lets go and the low back strains. Fix: lean back only a few centimetres, keep the chest lifted.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. It raises effort and blood pressure. Fix: slow nose breaths and count out-breaths.

commonMistakes.title: Pulling hard on the legs or hunching the shoulders
commonMistakes.text: Pulling hard on the legs or hunching the shoulders. Fix: hold the thighs lightly, shoulders down, or reach the arms forward.

commonMistakes.title: Cranking the neck or jutting the chin
commonMistakes.text: Cranking the neck or jutting the chin. It strains the neck. Fix: keep the gaze forward and the neck long.

commonMistakes.title: Letting the knees splay wide or the feet drop unevenly
commonMistakes.text: Letting the knees splay wide or the feet drop unevenly. It weakens the balance. Fix: knees together or hip-width, lift both feet together; a block between the knees can help.

commonMistakes.title: Dropping the feet quickly
commonMistakes.text: Dropping the feet quickly. Fix: lower slowly over 4 seconds.

commonMistakes.title: Holding too long on the first tries
commonMistakes.text: Holding too long on the first tries. Fix: start with 2 to 3 breaths and build up; stop when the form fades.

commonMistakes.title: Practising on a full stomach
commonMistakes.text: Practising on a full stomach. The pose presses on the stomach area. Fix: practise on a light or empty stomach.

safetyNotes: Firm belly, never pain. A strong, steady effort in the belly and the front of the hip is normal; sharp back pain, neck strain, or a pinch in the hip is not.

Back and neck: Yoga International (snippet) says not to practise the pose with a lumbar herniation, hernia or prolapse, and suggests a bent-knee or supported boat is a better route for low back issues. Tata AIA (snippet) advises avoiding it with spinal injuries or neck problems. Sources disagree on whether it helps chronic back pain. Keep the spine long; a collapsing back is the warning sign. Ask a doctor with a disc or spine problem.
Stomach and abdomen: PharmEasy and Dr Weil (snippets) list recent stomach surgery or ulcers as reasons to avoid it, since the pose presses on the stomach area. Practise on a light stomach.

Pregnancy: Art of Living (snippet) advises women to avoid the pose in pregnancy and in the first two days of the period; another source says to ask a doctor before any pregnancy exercise. Our choice: avoid it in pregnancy; ask a doctor for alternatives.
Postpartum and after surgery: a fixed wait after birth or surgery: Not found; sources agree on clearance from the provider first, especially after abdominal or caesarean surgery.

Osteoporosis: a Mayo Clinic-linked case series (PubMed 22448849; snippet, from the earlier Yoga & Stretch 20 research) raised concern about spinal flexion in osteopenia and osteoporosis; the search for boat pose and osteoporosis returned nothing. The Naukasana-specific verdict: Not found. Ask a doctor; if cleared, keep the spine long, avoid rounding, use bent knees and feet-down versions.

Blood pressure and heart: several sources (Dr Weil, Sportskeeda, a physician-guidance note; snippets) list high or low blood pressure, recent heart attack and heart conditions as cautions. Move slowly, never hold the breath, and ask a doctor first.
Other cautions: asthma, diarrhea, headaches, migraine and vertigo are listed by wellness sources (Dr Weil, PharmEasy, Sportskeeda; snippets). Clinical backing: Not found.
Stop immediately if you feel: sharp back, neck or hip pain, numbness or tingling, dizziness or faintness, chest pain or breathlessness, nausea, or pelvic, abdominal or incision pain.
Spotter: not needed. Gym etiquette: keep the mat out of walkways; do not hog the stretching area.

Start position: sitting versus lying on the back. We chose sitting (clear for the camera and the bent-knee form).
Hold time: 3 to 5 breaths, 15 to 30 seconds, or 2 to 5 breaths building to 10. We chose 4 breaths (about 20 s, est.), no breath-holding.
Spine cue: "straighten the spine" versus a slight pelvic roll back for the psoas. We chose a long spine with the tailbone heavy, no collapse and no hard arch.
Back pain: helps chronic back pain (one source) versus compresses the back and neck with poor form. We chose "modify: bent knees; ask a doctor".
Hernia: useful (Art of Living) versus avoid (Tata AIA, Yoga International). We chose avoid and ask a doctor.
Muscle emphasis: hip flexors dominate (yoga-anatomy sources) versus the abdominals as the main target (popular sources). We list both and note that a measured EMG study of Navasana was Not found.

Not found: Ministry of AYUSH Common Yoga Protocol, MDNIY and The Yoga Institute (Mumbai) Naukasana technique pages; a pose-specific MET; measured joint-angle norms for the held pose; EMG or trial evidence for this pose alone; an osteoporosis-specific verdict; a fixed wait after birth or surgery; clinical sources for cholesterol, thyroid, PCOS, knee pain, shoulder problems and heart disease for this pose. Our thresholds are estimates.
Most pages were seen only as search snippets or summaries; direct page fetches were not possible.
